title: Zapier vs Make for Non-Technical Small Business Owners: Pick One
meta_description: Zapier vs Make for non-technical small business owners: 3 common workflows compared on ease, usage costs, errors and AI. See which to learn first.
quick_answer: Most non-technical small business owners should learn Zapier first. It's the quickest way to set up simple step-by-step automations, like sending form leads to a CRM with a Slack alert, and then leave them running. Choose Make if you think in flowcharts, need if/then branches or run high volumes, because it usually costs less per step as volume grows.
key_takeaways: Start with Zapier if your workflows run in a straight line (trigger, then action, then action) and you want the gentlest learning curve.
Start with Make if you think in flowcharts, need if/then branches or loops, or process hundreds or thousands of records a month.

The two tools count usage differently. Zapier mostly counts completed action steps as tasks. Make counts every module that runs, including the trigger, as an operation, and its newer plans bill these as credits.
Before you compare pricing pages, estimate your monthly usage: runs per month × steps that count, plus a buffer for retries and busy periods.
Break every workflow on purpose before you rely on it. Leave out a required field or disconnect an app, then see how each tool alerts you and lets you retry.
If you need to host your automations yourself, or you have a developer, look at n8n instead of either tool.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for small business owners who don't write code, want to automate everyday admin like leads, orders and payment follow-ups, and only have time to learn one automation tool well.
intro: Zapier and Make both connect the apps you already use, so information moves between them without copying and pasting. Both are sold as no-code, which makes it hard to tell from their websites which one suits a busy owner who isn't technical. This guide compares them using three workflows almost every small business needs. The first sends a new web form entry to your CRM and posts a Slack alert. The second logs each Shopify order in Google Sheets. The third sends a thank-you email when an invoice is paid. For each one, you'll see how it's built in each tool, how it uses up your plan allowance, what happens when it breaks and where AI steps fit in. Features, plan names and prices change often, so use the plan details here as a starting point and confirm them on zapier.com and make.com before you buy.

steps.name: List the three jobs you'd automate first
steps.text: Write down the repetitive tasks that take up the most of your week, such as copying form leads into your CRM, logging orders or sending thank-you emails after payment. Circle the three that happen most often. Those are your test workflows.

steps.name: Sketch each workflow as boxes and arrows
steps.text: Draw the trigger, then each action. A straight line (trigger, then action, then action) suits Zapier. Forks such as 'if VIP, do this; otherwise do that', loops over order line items, or a lot of data clean-up suit Make.

steps.name: Estimate your monthly usage
steps.text: For each workflow, multiply the number of runs per month by the steps that count toward usage. In Zapier, that's usually the action steps. In Make, it's every module, including the trigger. Add about a 20% buffer for tests, retries and busy weeks.

steps.name: Open free accounts on both tools
steps.text: Zapier and Make both offer free tiers for testing. Check each vendor's site for the current limits, such as monthly tasks or credits, how many steps a workflow can have, and how often workflows check for new data.

steps.name: Build the same simple workflow in each tool
steps.text: Build form to CRM to Slack in both tools, using a private Slack channel such as #automation-test. Notice which tool's words and layout made sense without searching the help docs. That's a strong sign of which one you'll keep using.

steps.name: Break the workflow on purpose
steps.text: Submit a form with the email field left blank, then disconnect the Slack connection and run it again. Check how each tool tells you something failed, whether you can see what went wrong and how easily you can retry the failed run.

steps.name: Check your numbers against current pricing pages
steps.text: Use your usage estimate to find the right plan on each vendor's pricing page. Also check which features need a paid plan: multi-step workflows, branching (such as Zapier Paths), premium apps and how often workflows can check for new data.

steps.name: Commit to one tool and document every workflow
steps.text: Rebuild your top three workflows in the tool you chose. For each one, keep a short note covering what triggers it, what it does, which account each app connection uses and who to tell if it fails. A shared page in a workspace such as Notion works well for this.

rows: Learning curve
Gentler. You build a vertical list of steps, and each one asks a plain-language question.
Steeper at first. You build on a visual canvas and need to learn modules, bundles and the mapping panel.
How usage is counted
Tasks: usually each completed action step. Triggers and some built-in steps such as filters don't count.
Operations, billed as credits on newer plans: every module that runs, including the trigger. Checks for new data can count even when nothing new arrives.
Branching and loops
Filters, plus Paths for branches (check which plans include Paths). Fine for simple logic.
Routers, filters, iterators and aggregators are part of the standard canvas. Strong for complex logic.
Seeing what happened
Zap history lists each run and the data used at each step.
'Run once' shows data moving through each module. Click any module to see what went in and what came out.
Error handling
Run history, failure emails, automatic retry (Autoreplay) on some plans and custom error steps.
Error-handler routes on any module (Ignore, Resume, Break, Rollback, Commit), plus a list of incomplete runs you can retry.
AI steps
Built-in AI steps, AI app connections, an AI helper that drafts Zaps from a description, and agents.
Modules for major AI providers, AI agents and an AI building helper. Flexible inside larger workflows.
Cost as volume grows
Easy to predict at low volume. Usually costs more per step as volume grows.
Usually more usage per dollar at high volume, even though more steps count per run.

sections.heading: Zapier vs Make for non-technical small business owners: the short verdict
paragraphs: Zapier is the better first tool for most non-technical owners. Make is the better first tool for owners who think in flowcharts or expect high volume.

The real difference isn't which apps each tool connects. It's how each one feels to build in and how each one bills you. Zapier shows a workflow, called a Zap, as a vertical list: one trigger followed by actions. Make shows a workflow, called a scenario, as a canvas of connected circles called modules. You can branch, loop and rearrange them.

Both tools can build all three workflows in this guide without code, and both have free tiers for testing. App lists, plan limits and prices change often, so check current details on zapier.com and make.com before you commit.
bullets: Choose Zapier if your workflows run step by step in a straight line, you want the easiest learning curve, and you'd rather pay a bit more per step than spend time tinkering.
Choose Make if you think visually, your workflows branch (for example, 'if VIP customer, do X; otherwise do Y'), or you process a lot of records each month.
Skip both and look at n8n if you need to host your automations yourself, have strict rules about where data is stored, or have a developer on hand.
Still unsure? Start with Zapier for one workflow. The core ideas (triggers, actions and mapping fields between apps) carry over to Make if you switch later.

sections.heading: The three workflows used in this comparison
paragraphs: The three test workflows cover most small-business automation needs: capturing leads, logging sales and following up on payments.

Workflow 1, form to CRM to Slack, has three steps in both tools. A new response in a form tool such as Typeform, Jotform or Google Forms triggers it. The next step creates or updates a contact in a CRM such as HubSpot. The last step posts a message in Slack. It's just as easy to build in either tool, but Zapier's prompts walk a first-timer through each choice more directly.

Workflow 2, Shopify order to Google Sheets, gets tricky because of line items, since one order can contain several products. One row per order is easy in both tools. For one row per product, Make uses an Iterator module that splits the order into separate items and adds a row for each one. You can see that split clearly on the canvas, but every extra row uses more of your allowance. Zapier can also handle line items, but it's harder to see how the data is being split.

Workflow 3, invoice paid to thank-you email, usually starts with a QuickBooks Online 'new payment' trigger. A search step then finds the customer's email address, and a Gmail or Outlook 'send email' action finishes it. If you want different emails for first-time and repeat customers, the workflow needs a branch. Zapier handles this with Paths (check which plans include it), and Make handles it with a Router and filters.
bullets: Form to CRM to Slack: a straight line that suits either tool.
Shopify to Google Sheets: simple at one row per order. Make shows the split more clearly at one row per product.
Invoice paid to email: simple until you add branches, which is where Make's Router feels more natural.

sections.heading: How to build form to CRM to Slack in each tool
paragraphs: The setup steps are the same in both tools: pick a trigger, connect your accounts, map fields and switch the workflow on. The screens look very different, though. Exact button names change from time to time, so use these steps as a guide.

In Zapier, create a new Zap, choose your form app as the trigger and select an event such as 'New Response'. Connect your account, then click Test to pull in a sample entry. Next, add a CRM action such as 'Create or Update Contact' and fill the email, name and message fields by picking them from the sample data. Test that step, then add a Slack action that sends a channel message. Finally, publish the Zap, because it won't run until it's switched on.

In Make, create a new scenario, click the large plus button and add your form app's 'watch responses' module. Connect your account and choose where to start, for example only entries from now on. Next, add your CRM module and then a Slack 'Create a Message' module. Map fields by clicking items in the mapping panel. Click 'Run once', submit a test entry and watch the data move through each module. Then set the schedule and switch the scenario on.
Test with a realistic entry, such as a long message, an accented name or a phone number with spaces, not just 'test test'. Messy real-world data is what usually breaks automations after launch.
bullets: Pitfall: forgetting to switch the workflow on. Neither tool runs a draft workflow on its own.
Pitfall: typing a sample value into a field instead of mapping the live field. Every lead then gets the same name.
Pitfall: testing in a busy team Slack channel. Use a private #automation-test channel until the workflow is ready.
Pitfall: connecting apps with a personal login. Use a shared business account so the workflow keeps running if someone leaves.

sections.heading: Learning curve: which tool is easier to learn first?
paragraphs: Zapier is easier to learn, because each step asks a plain question: which app, which event, which account and which fields to fill.

Zapier also has an AI helper that can draft a Zap from a plain-English description, such as 'when someone fills in my Typeform, add them to HubSpot and tell me in Slack'. It's a useful starting point, but check every mapped field before you switch the Zap on. Check whether the helper is included in your plan.

Make asks you to learn a few ideas before it pays off. Data moves between modules in bundles. You map data from earlier modules using a panel. The scenario has one schedule and has to be switched on before it runs. Once these ideas make sense, Make's visibility is a real advantage: clicking any module shows exactly what went in and what came out, so finding a problem is quicker.
A simple test: if a flowchart of your business makes you feel calm, Make will probably suit you. If it makes you want to close the tab, start with Zapier.
bullets: Zapier terms: Zap, trigger, action, task, Zap history, Paths.
Make terms: scenario, module, bundle, operation or credit, Router, Iterator, Aggregator.
In both tools, you connect each app once and reuse that connection across workflows.

sections.heading: Tasks vs operations: how usage and costs grow
paragraphs: Zapier counts tasks, which are usually completed action steps. Make counts operations, billed as credits on its newer plans, for every module that runs, including the trigger.

In Zapier, the trigger generally doesn't count, and neither do some built-in steps such as filters. If a filter stops a run, the steps after it don't use tasks. In Make, every module that runs counts. Some features, including certain AI features, can use more than one credit. Scheduled triggers can use an operation each time they check for new data, even when nothing has arrived. Instant (webhook) triggers avoid this. An Iterator multiplies usage, because every module after it runs once for each item. Check each vendor's help centre for the current rules.

Here are rough usage figures for the three workflows. Check them against your own run history. Form to CRM to Slack is about 2 Zapier tasks or 3 Make operations per submission. Shopify to Sheets at one row per order is about 1 task or 2 operations. Invoice paid to email with a customer lookup is about 2 tasks or 3 operations.

At low volume, the cost difference rarely matters, and a few dozen runs a month may fit a free or entry-level plan on either tool. The gap opens as volume grows. For example, 300 form submissions a month is about 600 Zapier tasks or 900 Make operations. Make's plans usually include more operations per dollar than Zapier's include tasks, so Make often still costs less. Your time counts too: if Make saves a little money but takes three extra evenings to learn, it may not be worth it yet.
bullets: Check how many tasks or credits each plan includes per month.
Check what happens when you go over: whether workflows pause, you're charged extra, or you're moved to a higher plan.
Check how often each plan lets workflows check for new data.
Check whether the apps you need are labelled premium or are only on higher plans.
After a week of real use, compare your estimate with each tool's usage dashboard.

sections.heading: Error handling: what happens when a workflow breaks
paragraphs: Zapier makes errors easy to spot and retry. Make gives you finer control over what happens when a step fails, but you have to set it up yourself.

Zapier records every run in Zap history and emails you when a step fails. Some plans include Autoreplay, which retries failed steps automatically. Custom error handling lets you add a backup step, such as sending yourself a Slack message, when something fails. Zapier may switch off a Zap after repeated errors. Check which of these features your plan includes.

In Make, you can attach an error-handler route to any module and choose a behaviour: Ignore, Resume, Break, Rollback or Commit. If you enable incomplete executions in the scenario settings, Break saves the failed run so you can fix the problem and retry it. Make may also deactivate a scenario after repeated errors, so check those settings.
Before you rely on any workflow, break it on purpose. Submit a form with no email address and see what happens at the CRM step. Five minutes of testing teaches you more than any feature list.
bullets: Expired app connections: reconnect them, and set a reminder to check connections every few months.
Missing required fields: add a filter so incomplete entries stop before they reach the CRM.
Duplicate CRM contacts: choose a 'create or update' action instead of 'create'.
Edited Shopify orders: check whether your trigger fires on new orders only or on updates too, to avoid duplicate rows.
Renamed Google Sheets columns: don't rename or reorder columns that a workflow writes to.

sections.heading: AI steps in Zapier and Make
paragraphs: Both tools let you add AI steps that summarise, sort or draft text inside a workflow. Zapier's AI tools are more guided. Make's are separate building blocks that you combine yourself.

Zapier offers built-in AI steps, connections to ChatGPT and other AI providers, an AI helper that drafts Zaps and Zapier Agents for more independent tasks. Make offers modules for providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic (Claude) and Google (Gemini), plus AI agents and an AI building helper. Names and availability change, so check each vendor's current feature pages.
AI steps can cost money in two ways. They count toward your tasks or credits, and some setups also need your own API key from the AI provider, which comes with a separate bill.

In these three workflows, AI is most useful in two places. It can label each form lead as hot, warm or cold before the Slack alert, and it can personalise the thank-you email. For anything that goes to customers, have AI write a draft for you to review first. Only switch to automatic sending once you trust the results.
bullets: Good first AI uses: sorting leads, summarising long form answers and tidying messy data.
Higher-risk use: sending AI-written emails to customers without a person checking them.
Check how many tasks or credits an AI step uses before you run it at volume.

sections.heading: Who should skip both and look at n8n
paragraphs: Teams that need to host their own automations, or that have a developer on hand, should look at n8n instead of Zapier or Make.

n8n is a workflow automation tool with a visual canvas similar to Make's. You can run it on your own server or pay for n8n's cloud service. Its cloud pricing has been based on full workflow runs rather than individual steps, which can suit long workflows. Check n8n's current pricing and licence terms.

The trade-off is responsibility. If you host it yourself, someone has to handle setup, updates, security, backups and fixing problems. A developer can connect almost any app through n8n's HTTP Request node, but there are fewer polished ready-made connections for niche apps. For a solo owner without technical help, the extra work usually outweighs the savings.
bullets: Consider n8n if customer data must stay on servers you control.
Consider n8n if you run very long or very frequent workflows and per-step pricing is getting expensive.
Consider n8n if a developer can take charge of hosting and maintenance.
Skip n8n if you just want a few workflows running by Friday. Zapier or Make will get you there faster.

recommendations.best_for: Non-technical owners who want simple step-by-step workflows, such as form to CRM to Slack, running quickly with guided setup and little ongoing maintenance.
recommendations.not_for: High-volume or heavily branching workflows where per-step costs add up quickly, or owners who want to see and adjust complex logic on a visual canvas.

recommendations.best_for: Visual thinkers and growing shops with branching logic, product-by-product order processing or high monthly volumes who want more usage per dollar.
recommendations.not_for: Owners who want to set things up once and forget them, and who don't want to learn terms like modules, bundles and iterators.

recommendations.best_for: Owners still chasing invoices by hand who want accounting software with built-in invoicing that can trigger thank-you or follow-up emails through Zapier or Make.
recommendations.not_for: Businesses already happy with another accounting platform. Both automation tools connect to many popular accounting apps, so switching just for this workflow rarely makes sense.

recommendations.best_for: Owners who want one shared place to record every automation: what triggers it, what it does, which account it uses and who to tell when it breaks.
recommendations.not_for: Teams that already keep process notes in another wiki or shared drive. Any shared document works for this, so it isn't worth adopting Notion just for this purpose.

faq.question: Is Make harder to learn than Zapier?
faq.answer: Yes. Most non-technical users take longer to learn Make, because they first need to understand modules, bundles and data mapping on a visual canvas. Once those ideas make sense, many people find Make easier for complex workflows, because they can see the whole flow and check the data at every step.

faq.question: Is Make cheaper than Zapier?
faq.answer: Make is usually cheaper at higher volumes, because its plans generally include more operations per dollar than Zapier's plans include tasks. Make also counts more steps per run, including the trigger, so compare the two using your own monthly usage estimate. Prices change, so check current plans on both vendors' websites.

faq.question: What is the difference between a Zapier task and a Make operation?
faq.answer: A Zapier task is usually one completed action step. Triggers and some built-in steps, such as filters, don't count. A Make operation is any module that runs, including the trigger. Make's newer plans bill operations as credits, and some features, such as certain AI features, can use more than one credit.

faq.question: Can I move my workflows from Zapier to Make later?
faq.answer: There's no simple one-click transfer, so expect to rebuild your workflows by hand. The core ideas (triggers, actions, filters and field mapping) carry over directly. A short written description of each workflow makes rebuilding much quicker.

faq.question: Do I need to know how to code to use Zapier or Make?
faq.answer: No. You can build workflows like form to CRM, Shopify to Google Sheets and invoice-paid emails in either tool without code. Code only helps with unusual data clean-up or apps without a ready-made connection, and both tools offer no-code workarounds for many of those cases.

faq.question: Is n8n free?
faq.answer: n8n has a version you can host yourself, but running it still costs money for a server and time for setup, updates and security. It also has a paid cloud service. Check n8n's current licence and pricing to confirm whether your use is covered.

conclusion: For most non-technical small business owners choosing a first automation tool, Zapier is the place to start if your workflows run in a straight line and you want them to just work. Choose Make if you think visually, need branches or loops, or expect your volume to grow. Before you pay for either one, build the same real workflow in both free tiers, break it on purpose, and check your usage estimate against each vendor's current pricing page. Then commit to one tool, write down how each workflow works, and add your next automation only after the first one has run cleanly for a few weeks.
